item.title: Twenty Years of data from the RAPID-MOCHA-WBTS array: Long-Term Changes in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, Heat and Freshwater Transports
item.dc:creator: Tillys Petit, Shane Elipot, David A. Smeed, William E. Johns, Ryan H. Smith, Denis L. Volkov, … (+6)
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, overturning circulation, ocean circulation
Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) For over 20 years, measurements across the Atlantic at 26° N has continuously recorded the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation that carry heat northward and help shape the climate. This paper describes the resulting data, how they are produced and shared, and how they show changes in these ocean circulation over time. It also releases the computer code used to produce them, so anyone can reproduce and reuse the data.

item.title: A multi-decadal dataset of surface damage on Antarctic ice shelves (1999–2024)
item.dc:creator: Leyue Tang, Jonathan L. Bamber, Tian Li, Gang Qiao
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: ice shelf, Antarctic, sea level, sea-level rise
Many Antarctic ice shelves are thinning and retreating, threatening future sea-level rise. Surface damage indicates structural weakening, but long-term records are scarce. We created a multi-decadal surface damage record for nine representative Antarctic ice shelves using satellite imagery and deep learning. Among them, Pine Island, Thwaites and Scar Inlet have experienced the most significant changes in surface damage during the study period, providing insights into ice shelf stability.

item.title: Sub-daily multi-pass AMSR2 passive microwave response to the 2012 extreme melt event in northwestern Greenland
item.dc:creator: Takumi Suzuki, Tomonori Tanikawa, Rigen Shimada, Misako Kachi
item.description:
Frontiers in Remote Sensing — matched: ice sheet, Greenland, surface energy balance, firn
The unprecedented Greenland Ice Sheet melt in summer 2012 provides a natural experiment to evaluate how spaceborne passive microwave brightness temperature ( T B ) responds to extreme melt on diurnal timescales. We analyzed multi-frequency AMSR2 T B from GCOM–W over a northwestern Greenland site (SIGMA–A) and compared the radiometric evolution with in situ snow temperatures and surface energy balance terms derived from automated weather station meteorology. From early to mid-July 2012, T B showed coherent, frequency- and polarization-dependent transitions through the major melt event, including a pronounced shift in diurnal behavior. Outside the melt peak, high-frequency T B (36.5 and 89.0 GHz) exhibited clear day–night contrast, whereas during the extreme melt period T B remained elevated with a strongly damped diurnal range, consistent with sustained nighttime wetness. At 89.0 GHz, T B increases coincided with persistently positive surface energy input dominated by enhanced downward longwave radiation and peak cloud occurrence inferred from Aqua/MODIS and all-sky imagery, supporting a cloud-linked high-frequency enhancement. In contrast, low-frequency T B (6.9–10.7 GHz) decreased, most strongly in H-pol, consistent with melt-driven reductions in effective emissivity associated with wet–dry dielectric contrasts. Most notably, the 6.9–7.3 GHz difference revealed a distinct polarization-dependent post-melt transition: after the melt peak, Δ T B, H showed increased variability and occasional positive values, whereas Δ T B, V remained nearly unchanged at negative values. This behavior indicates that the 6.9–7.3 GHz H-pol pair is sensitive not only to melt-driven changes in low-frequency emission, but also to refreezing-modified near-surface stratigraphy. These results demonstrate that multi-frequency microwave radiometry can resolve rapid snow–firn transitions during extreme melt and identify the 6.9–7.3 GHz H-pol difference as a compact diagnostic that complements conventional melt monitoring by capturing post-melt near-surface structural evolution.

item.title: Modelling the effects of proglacial lake filling and drainage on lake-terminating glacier dynamics
item.dc:creator: Ankit Pramanik, Sarah L. Greenwood, Mathieu Morlighem, Jamie Barnett, Felicity A. Holmes, Richard Gyllencreutz, … (+1)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: ice sheet, glacier, mass loss
Ice sheet/glacier retreat is driving expansion of glacial lakes impounded at the ice margin. Using an ice sheet model, we find that lake filling and drainage causes systematic changes to glacier thickness, velocity and mass loss. Rising lake levels dramatically increase mass loss as the ice margin becomes buoyant, while rapid lake drainage can drive crevassing and destabilise the margin. Steady lake drainage, in contrast, has a stabilising effect, and may mitigate mass loss and flood hazards.

item.title: Milanković’s Theory of Ice Ages and Serbian Loess
item.dc:creator: Milivoj B. Gavrilov
item.description:
Quaternary — matched: albedo, interglacial, insolation
The text deals with Milanković’s Mathematical–Astronomical Theory of Ice Ages and its connection with Serbian loess. Here it is recalled, put into the context of the people who collaborated with Milanković during his work (W. Köppen, A. Wegener, V. Mišković, W. Jardetzky, D. Mitrinović, and S. Fempl), and it points to its 50th anniversary of verification in the journal Science. Then, the Theory is compared with magnetic susceptibility (MS) profiles of two Serbian loess–paleosol sequences (Mošorin and Stari Slankamen) by (i) showing side-by-side the Milanković’s Insolation Curves and the MS Curves over the last 600,000 years and (ii) discussing the relation of the MS spectral components and the orbital (eccentricity, obliquity, and precession) and terrestrial (solar constant and albedo) forcing of Milankovic’sTheory. In addition to the similarities between Milanković’s Insolation Curves and the MS Curves, there are discrepancies, the causes of which are analyzed in detail. The text ends with a biographical section on Milanković’s voyages down the Danube and the StariSlankamen profile, where in the layers of loess there are visual traces of the change in glacial (Ice Ages), cold intervals and interglacial (Inter Ice Ages), warm intervals in the geological history of the Earth. These traces match relatively well with Milanković’s Insolation Curves, which he could not have known during his many passes. In the conclusion, suggestions are given on how to reduce the discrepancies between Milanković’s Insolation Curves and the MS Curves and thereby improve paleoclimatological research.

item.title: Disentangling positional change from intensity in the palaeoclimate reconstruction of circulation patterns
item.dc:creator: Edward Forman, Zoë Thomas, Paul D.M. Hughes, Mark D. Peaple
item.description:
Communications Earth & Environment — matched: paleoclimate, proxy, climate change
Abstract Under ongoing anthropogenic climate change, the impacts of forcing on climate circulation patterns, such as ocean currents and wind belts, are an area of particular scientific interest. Due to the complexity of the system, these subsystem patterns can exhibit multi-dimensional variability such as strength change or feature migration. However, conventional proxy-based reconstructions risk conflating positional shifts with intensity changes, thereby obscuring the true mode of past variability and potentially impeding the accuracy of hindcasts and predictions. Here, we present this issue and discuss three subsystems where previous work has attempted to disentangle spatial and magnitudinal change, namely the Gulf Stream, Intertropical Convergence Zone, and Southern Hemisphere westerly winds. Our analysis of deployed methodologies finds that studies principally employ spatial networks and dimension-specific proxies to separate these compounding effects. We emphasise the importance of incorporating this interpretation challenge into future study design and highlight the need for new disentanglement methods. This review synthesises existing disentanglement approaches, provides a concise conceptual framing, and offers practical recommendations for study design.

item.title: How abruptly did the Holocene Green Sahara end?
item.dc:creator: Martin Claussen, Anne Dallmeyer, Frank Darius, Philipp Hoelzmann, Michèle Dinies
item.description:
Climate of the Past — matched: Holocene, proxy
To move the long-standing debate of whether the vegetation changes in the Sahara during the last 8000 years occurred abruptly or gradually we propose a new quantitative metric. Our analysis of model and proxy data suggests the vegetation composition in the Holocene Sahara can undergo substantially more abrupt transitions than total vegetation cover, and a gradual expansion of the Sahara can be accompanied by abrupt, step-like transitions within local ecosystems.

item.title: Run it Back: Autoregression vs. Video Diffusion for Final-Conditioned Weather Trajectories
item.dc:creator: Jerry Lin, Elizabeth A. Barnes
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: emulator, ensemble, heat wave
arXiv:2611.21521v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Low-likelihood, high-impact extremes are projected to increase in severity and frequency in a warming climate. Sampling the precursors that lead to these events traditionally requires massive ensembles that scale poorly with lead time and rarity, and typical rare-event sampling and ensemble-boosting methods do not show how a single extreme might arise from diverse synoptic precursors. Recently, Lin et al.\ (2026) showed this is possible with final-conditioned 66-hour trajectories (trajectories constrained to end at an observed state) from cBottle-video, a pre-trained, off-the-shelf video diffusion climate emulator not explicitly fine-tuned for this task (Brenowitz et al., 2025). However, its ensembles were underdispersed and geostrophically inconsistent, and it reproduces conditioned frames only approximately, hindering autoregressive rollout. Here, we train Rewind-AR, a backward-in-time probabilistic autoregressive model with a FourCastNet~3 backbone (Bonev et al., 2025), and generate final-conditioned ensembles for the same three cases: the 2021 Pacific Northwest heatwave, Hurricane Ian, and Superstorm Sandy (in the Supplementary Information). The leading modes of Rewind-AR's antecedent 500 hPa geopotential height explain far more of the across-member variance than cBottle-video's for both hurricane position and heatwave surface temperature, and Rewind-AR better reproduces the day-over-day heatwave intensification observed in ERA5. Finally, geostrophic inconsistencies close to the conditioning frame seen in cBottle-video are not reproduced by Rewind-AR. Nevertheless, up to 22\% of Rewind-AR members become numerically unstable within 66 hours, so improving rollout physical consistency and stability over long lead times is a natural next step.

item.title: Climate and glacier geometry dominate global glacier–lake interactions
item.dc:creator: Shaochun Zhao, Guoqing Zhang, Matthias Huss, Georg Veh, Jonathan L. Carrivick, Tobias Bolch, … (+11)
item.description:
Nature Climate Change — matched: glacier, mass loss, climate change
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02808-5 The contribution of glacial lakes to glacier mass loss is unclear. This work maps global glacial lakes in 2000 and 2020 to quantify changes in number, volume and area, showing that they explain 11 ± 7% of lake-terminating glacier loss, with climate forcing and glacier geometry the dominant factors.

item.title: Seasonal biases induced by illumination changes and shadow casting in remote sensing derived glacier flow velocities
item.dc:creator: Laurane Charrier, Nathan Lioret, Fanny Brun, Amaury Dehecq, Romain Millan, Anuar Togaibekov, … (+3)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: glacier, remote sensing
Sub-annual glacier surface velocity derived from remote sensing images are receiving increasing attention. In the meantime, systematic seasonal errors (i.e. biases) have been reported in time series derived from optical images on various landforms, such as landslides or dunes. The extent to which such biases affect glacier velocity maps remains poorly investigated. Here, we propose characterizing the amplitude and spatial distribution of these seasonal biases.

item.title: The 4-mode Modal Aerosol Module in C+ + (MAM4xx) v1.0: representing prognostic aerosols in a global cloud-system resolving atmosphere model for GPU exascale computing
item.dc:creator: Jerome D. Fast, Balwinder Singh, Oscar Diaz-Ibarra, Jeff Johnson, Chandru Dhandapani, Brian Gaudet, … (+12)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: Earth system model, Earth system
We ported a prognostic representation of aerosols to C++ and integrated it into an Earth system model that runs on powerful GPU supercomputers. The code conversion approach keeps the same detailed physics as the Fortran version, was carefully tested, and results show that new code produces aerosol simulations consistent with real‑world data over the central U.S. in spring 2016. Future work will optimize the code for GPUs so to reduce the overall computational time.

item.title: Evaluation of machine-learning and deep-learning SPEI drought forecasts against persistence across timescales and lead times in Bangladesh
item.dc:creator: Mahir Ahnaf, Showmitra Kumar Sarkar
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: reanalysis, machine learning
arXiv:2611.25075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bangladesh, home to nearly 178 million people, is highly vulnerable to recurring droughts that threaten food security and rural livelihoods. Machine-learning and deep-learning models are increasingly used to forecast drought indices such as the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI). Most studies report accuracy without a persistence reference, although accumulated indices are strongly autocorrelated, and seldom test drought detection, longer leads or variation between training runs. This study forecast SPEI at 3-, 6- and 12-month timescales one to three months ahead for the eight divisions of Bangladesh, using ERA5 reanalysis checked against 35 Bangladesh Meteorological Department stations. Five models, XGBoost, CNN, Bi-LSTM, CNN-BiLSTM and CEEMDAN-BiLSTM, were trained with five seeds each, scored on accuracy, skill against persistence and drought detection, and interpreted with Shapley values. At a one-month lead, the CNN-BiLSTM and Bi-LSTM beat persistence clearly at SPEI-3 and SPEI-6 (skill 0.408 and 0.350), while at SPEI-12 a Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.872 barely exceeded persistence (0.850). Skill and detection could disagree: at SPEI-3 and a three-month lead, XGBoost had the highest skill (0.439) yet detected none of the 119 drought months. Only at SPEI-6 did the forecasts beat persistence significantly and match its detection at all three leads, with fewer false alarms. At SPEI-12, gains were small or absent and varied between seeds. The forecasts kept 76-80% of their correlation against station-derived SPEI and relied mainly on precipitation and lagged SPEI. Forecasts should therefore be judged on skill against persistence and detection across several seeds, not on accuracy alone. In Bangladesh, SPEI-6 forecasts can support early warning up to three months ahead and SPEI-3 forecasts one month ahead, while SPEI-12 is better suited to monitoring.

item.title: Exploring the Cenozoic Earth system with extraterrestrial 3He
item.dc:creator: Jordan T. Abell, Frank J. Pavia, Jennifer L. Middleton, Gisela Winckler
item.description:
Climate of the Past — matched: Earth system
Marine sediments provide a unique window into Earth's past, preserving material derived from deserts, volcanoes, rivers, ocean life, and even space. Quantifying how quickly these materials accumulate over time can reveal changes in past environments. Traditional methods for calculating accumulation rates can be unreliable, but another approach that uses minute space dust particles offers a more accurate way to track long-term changes in the Earth system.

item.title: SISAL_monv1: a global database of cave monitoring observations
item.dc:creator: Pauline C. Treble, Yining Zang, Nikita Kaushal, István G. Hatvani, Péter Tanos, Zoltan Kern, … (+11)
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: paleoclimate
Water dripping from cave ceilings is studied to understand how water moves from the surface to the cave. This has applications for palaeoclimate, groundwater and cave conservation studies. We present a new database containing water isotope measurements for drip water and rainfall at 75 cave locations globally. The database is a SISAL working group initiative (Speleothem Isotopes Synthesis and AnaLysis) and complements cave speleothem databases previously constructed by SISAL.

item.title: GPROF V08: Improving Satellite Precipitation Estimates Across a Heterogeneous Constellation of Passive-Microwave Sensors
item.dc:creator: Simon Pfreundschuh, Paula J. Brown, Christian D. Kummerow
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: Bayesian, neural network
arXiv:2611.19978v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Precipitation estimates from the passive microwave observations (PMW) of the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission serve a wide range of scientific, societal, and economic applications. The Goddard Profiling Algorithm (GPROF) is the operational precipitation retrieval used to produce the level-two precipitation estimates for the GPM mission. This study presents GPROF V08 - the most recent version of GPROF and a major update aimed at improving the accuracy of precipitation estimates from the GPM constellation. GPROF V08 replaces the single-pixel Bayesian retrieval scheme used by earlier GPROF versions with a convolutional neural network (CNN). Implementing the algorithm for the full GPM constellation required addressing several challenges such as the generation of synthetic observations suitable for training CNN retrievals, which has been described in the first part of this two-part study. This second part describes the final, operational implementation of GPROF V08, which adds a finetuning stage to the training to overcome remaining uncertainties in the synthetic training data. We extensively validate the new GPROF V08 algorithm for principal GPM sensors against reference precipitation estimates from combined radar and radiometer retrievals from GPM and TRMM as well as independent ground-based reference measurements. While the magnitude of improvements varies by sensor and surface type, the retrieval accuracy for all assessed sensors is improved. Although challenges such as the persistence of climatological biases (which remain of the same order as for GPROF V07) persist, GPROF V08 constitutes a substantial advancement in spaceborne precipitation monitoring. Since the improvements are robust across all assessed GPM sensors, the update is expected to improve the full historical GPM precipitation record and thus benefit a wide range of downstream datasets and applications.

item.title: Reconstrução da vegetação dos biomas brasileiros com baixo de CO2 atmosférico e a existência de fogo no Último Máximo Glacial
item.dc:creator: Clara Quadros do Amaral, Henderson Silva Wanderley
item.description:
Revista Brasileira de Climatologia — matched: CO2
O Último Máximo Glacial representa o fim da última glaciação e é marcado pela redução na temperatura média de todo o globo, em comparação as médias atuais. Nesse período, as flutuações climáticas causaram mudanças na vegetação. No entanto, uma análise que leve em consideração a influencia da baixa concentração de dióxido de carbono (CO2) atmosférico e fogo sobre a vegetação são escassos. Frente a isso, o presente estudo pretende reconstruir a vegetação dos biomas brasileiros para cenários distintos, com diferentes nível de CO2 atmosférico e a existência fogo no Último Máximo Glacial (UMG) e no período Pré-Industrial (PI). Para tanto, foi utilizada como metodologia a simulação de reconstruções da cobertura da vegetação, o modelo Land-surface Process and exchanges (LPX), com dados do modelo Miroc de circulação geral da atmosfera. Foram avaliados quatro cenário de reconstrução da vegetação dos biomas brasileiros, para o período pré-industrial e para o UMG, com mudança da variação da concentração atmosférica de CO2 e a existência de incêndios florestais. Os resultados mostraram fragmentação da vegetação, sobretudo para a redução das florestas tropicais e temperadas, com árvores de grandes portes, substituídas por florestas menos adensadas, com dossel aberto ou regiões com vegetação rasteira ou até mesmo desérticas. A hipótese de aparecimento de Refúgios Amazônicos foi verificado. A mudança na concentração do CO2 e a existência de fogo podem acelerar o processo de fragmentação da vegetação dos biomas brasileiros, acelerando o processo de savanização

item.title: FluidUrban v1.0: enhancing urban ventilation and pollutant dispersion modelling with three-dimensional dynamic adaptive meshes optimisation
item.dc:creator: Xiaofei Wu, Siyang Chen, Jinxi Li, Yu Zhang, Zifa Wang, Pu Gan, … (+2)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: numerical method
Cities face a major challenge in tracking how wind and air pollution move through complex building clusters. Common numerical models often struggle to balance accuracy with calculating speed. We developed a new simulation system that automatically adjusts its focus to where the air is moving rapidly. By testing this against observations, it significantly improves predictions of wind and pollution. This tool helps urban planners design healthier cities by better identifying how pollutants travel.

item.title: Lake Ice Thickness retrieval using TanDEM-X immediate interferometry
item.dc:creator: Peilin Chen, Grant Gunn, Sukhdip Kharoud
item.description:
The Cryosphere
Given our recent advances in understanding the interaction between lake ice and radar, it has become possible to use radar satellites to measure lake ice thickness. We developed detailed methods for lake ice measurement and compared them with field measurements and thermal-based simulations. Results demonstrated our method can be used to accurately measure ice thickness. The use of recently launched and future satellites is expected to yield more precise measurements using this method.

item.title: Species-resolved inventory of forest biogenic volatile organic emissions across China with MEGAN v3.2
item.dc:creator: Hao Liu, Hao Xu, Yixin Huang, Wei Zhou, Yunting Xiao, Qinghao Guo, … (+5)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
To better track natural emissions from forests, we built a detailed model covering 234 tree species across China – far more precise than past methods that lumped all trees into broad categories. The study found that planting different tree species in the same location can produce very different emission patterns, affecting haze and ozone formation in distinct ways. These findings suggest that thoughtful species selection can help balance carbon goals with cleaner air.
